title: Quản Lý Nghiệp (Karmic Management: What Goes Around Comes Around in Your Business and Your Life)
author: Geshe Michael Roach, Lama Christie McNally, and Michael Gordon
summary:
*Karmic Management* (published in Vietnamese as *Quản Lý Nghiệp*) is the sequel to Geshe Michael Roach's bestselling business-Buddhism book *The Diamond Cutter*, co-written with Lama Christie McNally and Michael Gordon, the founder of the hair-care company Bumble and bumble. Where *The Diamond Cutter* told the origin story of applying ancient Buddhist principles to build a successful diamond business, *Karmic Management* is designed as a short, practical companion: a step-by-step system, described by the authors as readable in under an hour, for applying the same principles to any business or personal goal.

The book's central argument rests on karma — not as an abstract or purely religious concept, but reframed as a practical business principle: that helping others succeed (customers, suppliers, coworkers, even competitors) is what actually generates the conditions for one's own success, rather than a zero-sum, self-interested approach to competition and negotiation. Each of the book's core lessons opens with a quotation drawn from ancient Buddhist texts, which the authors then translate into concrete, applicable guidance for a 21st-century business or personal context, illustrated with real anecdotes from their own entrepreneurial experience.

The book lays out what's often described as Eight Rules (or Steps) of Karmic Management, building from the idea of noticing what currently isn't working and being willing to stop repeating it, through finding the true underlying cause of problems (going deeper than the surface-level explanation), identifying trustworthy business and life partners, and ultimately taking responsibility for one's own actions and mental habits as the actual lever for changing outcomes, rather than trying to control external circumstances or other people directly.

Throughout, the authors are explicit that this isn't a soft or purely idealistic philosophy — it's presented as a hard-nosed, results-oriented business method, backed by their own commercial success, arguing that karmic cause-and-effect operates in business dealings just as reliably (if less visibly) as conventional cause-and-effect operates in physical processes, and that a business run on these principles produces both practical results and genuine wellbeing for everyone connected to it.

sections.title: Introduction — What Karma Actually Means in Business
sections.summary:
This opening chapter reframes karma away from a purely religious or fatalistic concept and toward a practical operating principle: that our own past actions (mental, verbal, and physical) plant seeds that shape what happens to us next, including in business.

The authors ground this in their own credibility — Roach's diamond-industry career built explicitly on these principles, and Gordon's growth of Bumble and bumble into a large, successful company — arguing that karmic management isn't abstract philosophy layered onto a business, but the actual operating system behind their own commercial results.

The chapter closes by previewing the book's Eight Rules, framed as a structured, learnable system rather than a loose set of aspirations.
keyLessons: Karma, as used in this book, refers to a practical cause-and-effect principle in business and life, not an abstract or purely religious idea.
The authors ground their claims in their own direct commercial success applying these principles.
The book presents karmic management as a structured, learnable system (Eight Rules), not vague philosophy.

sections.title: Rule One — Stop Doing What Isn't Working
sections.summary:
This chapter introduces the first rule: recognizing patterns of action that consistently fail to produce desired results, and having the discipline to actually stop them rather than repeating the same approach out of habit or hope.

The authors use business examples of repeated, ineffective strategies (a sales approach, a management habit) that persist simply because they're familiar, arguing that most people waste enormous energy "playing games of chance" with outcomes instead of honestly assessing what isn't working.

The chapter closes by connecting this to a broader theme: karmic management requires honest self-assessment before any external strategy can succeed.
keyLessons: Honestly identifying what habitually isn't working is the necessary first step before any other change.
Repeating familiar but ineffective strategies out of habit wastes significant energy.
Real change starts with self-assessment, not external strategy first.

sections.title: Rule Two — Find the Cause of the Cause
sections.summary:
This chapter pushes past surface-level explanations of a problem to its deeper, underlying root — going beyond the first, most obvious cause to what's really driving a recurring issue.

The authors illustrate with business scenarios where a surface fix (addressing a symptom) fails to resolve a recurring problem because the real underlying cause was never addressed, and connect this to Buddhist teaching about the layered, interdependent nature of cause and effect.

The chapter closes by encouraging readers to practice this "cause of the cause" inquiry on their own recurring business or personal frustrations.
keyLessons: Surface-level fixes often fail because they don't address the true underlying cause.
Recurring problems usually have a deeper root than the first, most obvious explanation.
Practicing "cause of the cause" inquiry is a repeatable diagnostic habit, not a one-time exercise.

sections.title: Rule Three — Identify Your True Business Partners
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses discernment in choosing who to build business and personal relationships with, emphasizing spiritual and ethical alignment as a practical, not just moral, consideration.

The authors argue that partnerships built without this discernment — chosen purely for short-term convenience or profit — tend to generate more long-term karmic (and practical) difficulty than partnerships built on shared values and mutual benefit.

The chapter closes by linking this rule back to the book's broader theme: who you choose to work with shapes the karmic seeds you're planting as much as what you do.
keyLessons: Choosing business partners based on shared values, not just short-term convenience, reduces long-term difficulty.
Partnership choices themselves function as karmic seeds, not just neutral logistical decisions.
Discernment in partnership is presented as a practical business skill, not only an ethical nicety.

sections.title: Rule Four — Start With Yourself
sections.summary:
This chapter argues that lasting change in any relationship or business outcome must begin with the practitioner's own actions and mental habits, rather than attempts to directly change other people's behavior.

The authors connect this to core Buddhist teaching on karma being generated by one's own actions, not controlled by trying to manipulate external people or circumstances, and give business examples of leaders who successfully shifted outcomes by changing their own conduct first.

The chapter closes by setting up the remaining rules as extensions of this same self-focused starting point.
keyLessons: Lasting change starts with the practitioner's own actions and habits, not attempts to control others.
Trying to directly change other people's behavior is presented as a less effective lever than self-change.
This principle underlies and connects to the book's remaining rules.
Deliberately helping business partners, customers, and even competitors succeed is presented as the core generative practice of karmic management.
Structured reflection or meditation is used as a tool for clarifying goals and interrupting unhelpful patterns.
Right livelihood — how you earn, not just how much — matters directly to long-term outcomes in this framework.
The Eight Rules are meant to function together continuously, not as a checklist completed once.
Reframe karma as a practical, in-business cause-and-effect principle, not just a religious or fatalistic concept.
Before changing strategy, honestly identify what habitual actions consistently aren't working, and stop repeating them.
Push past the first, most obvious explanation of a recurring problem to find its deeper underlying cause.
Choose business and life partners based on shared values and genuine alignment, not just short-term convenience.
Focus on changing your own actions and habits first, rather than trying to directly control other people's behavior.
Deliberately act to help customers, suppliers, and even competitors succeed as the core lever for your own success.
Use structured reflection or meditation to clarify goals and interrupt unhelpful patterns before they compound.
Pay attention to how you earn, not just how much, since the means of earning matters to long-term outcomes in this framework.
Treat these practices as an ongoing, continuous discipline rather than a one-time program.

quotes.text: Karma... is the real cause, the cause behind everything, everywhere, underneath everything, just like the earth of our Mother Earth is everywhere.
quotes.attribution: Michael Roach, Christie McNally, and Michael Gordon

quotes.text: Helping others become successful... is the real key to success in life as well as in business.
quotes.attribution: Michael Roach, Christie McNally, and Michael Gordon (as described in publisher materials)

whoThisIsFor: Business owners and professionals open to a Buddhist-influenced, ethics-first approach to business strategy, especially readers who enjoyed *The Diamond Cutter*.
whenToReadThis: As a short, practical follow-up after *The Diamond Cutter*, or when looking for a quick, principle-based reset on how to approach a difficult business relationship or negotiation.

authorBio.name: Geshe Michael Roach, Lama Christie McNally, and Michael Gordon
authorBio.bio:
Geshe Michael Roach is an American-born, fully ordained Buddhist monk who received his geshe (master's-level) degree from Sera Mey Tibetan Monastery after over twenty years of study, and who worked for many years as a director of a large New York diamond company while applying Buddhist principles to that business — an experience he chronicled in his bestselling first book, *The Diamond Cutter*. He founded the Asian Classics Institute and the Asian Classics Input Project, and has been involved in Tibetan monastery restoration work.

Lama Christie McNally is a co-founder of the Yoga Studies Institute and Diamond Mountain University in Arizona, and has co-authored several books with Roach on yoga and Buddhist practice in addition to this one.

Michael Gordon is an entrepreneur who founded and led Bumble and bumble, a large, commercially successful hair-products company, and brought his own direct entrepreneurial experience to the book's business examples and case studies.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Karmic Management
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The authors' central framework: applying the Buddhist principle that one's own past actions (mental, verbal, physical) shape future outcomes directly to business practice, arguing that helping others succeed is the actual generative cause of one's own success.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Eight Rules (Steps) of Karmic Management
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A structured sequence of practical principles — including stopping ineffective habitual actions, finding the true underlying cause of problems, choosing aligned business partners, and starting change with oneself — that together form the book's practical system, each opened with a supporting Buddhist textual quotation.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Cause of the Cause
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A diagnostic practice of pushing past the first, most obvious explanation for a recurring problem to identify its deeper, true underlying cause, drawn from Buddhist teaching on layered, interdependent causation.

actionSteps: Identify one recurring business or personal habit that consistently fails to produce the result you want, and commit to consciously stopping it for the next two weeks rather than repeating it out of routine.
For a current recurring frustration (with a client, colleague, or process), write down the obvious surface cause, then ask "what's the cause of that cause" at least twice more to find a deeper root.
List your current key business or life partnerships and honestly assess which are built on genuine shared values versus pure short-term convenience.
This week, take one deliberate action that helps a customer, supplier, or even a competitor succeed, without expecting an immediate return.
Set aside 10 minutes of quiet, structured reflection (without your phone) before a significant decision this week, specifically to clarify what you actually want from it.
reflectionQuestions: What is one habitual action in your business or life that you suspect isn't working, but that you keep repeating anyway?
Who are the people you currently do business with primarily out of convenience rather than genuine shared values?
Where in your work could you meaningfully help someone else succeed this month, even without a guaranteed return to you?

points: The book's central causal claim — that helping others succeed is what generates one's own success — is a religious and philosophical claim, not an empirically tested business principle, and the book relies primarily on the authors' own anecdotal success (Roach's diamond business, Gordon's Bumble and bumble) rather than controlled evidence for its effectiveness as a general business strategy.

Geshe Michael Roach and Lama Christie McNally have been the subject of significant public controversy regarding their teaching community and personal conduct (including scrutiny from within the Buddhist teaching community over their romantic and spiritual-partnership practices), which some readers may want to be aware of when evaluating the authors' broader credibility as spiritual teachers.

The book's format — very short, described by its own publisher as readable in under an hour — necessarily limits how deeply any of the Eight Rules can be explored or substantiated compared to a full-length business or spiritual text.

As a direct sequel positioned to capitalize on the commercial success of *The Diamond Cutter*, some critics have noted the book leans on that earlier book's credibility and brand recognition more than on independently demonstrating the new material's effectiveness.
criticalTake.contextNote: Interested readers should be aware that Geshe Michael Roach's teaching organization and personal practices have drawn public scrutiny and controversy within Western Buddhist circles in the years since this book's publication, separate from an assessment of the book's business content itself.

sourceNotes: Identified via web search as the Vietnamese translation of *Karmic Management: What Goes Around Comes Around in Your Business and Your Life* by Geshe Michael Roach, Lama Christie McNally, and Michael Gordon, the sequel to *The Diamond Cutter*; the eight-rule structure and general content were cross-checked against multiple Vietnamese bookseller/publisher pages (Thái Hà Books, sachhay.vinasite, sumenhkimcuong) which independently describe the same eight-chapter/eight-rule structure. Individual rule names for rules 5-8 were not independently confirmed with the same confidence as rules 1-4 and are presented as a reasonable synthesis of the book's known themes (positive seed-planting, meditation/reflection, right livelihood, sustained practice) rather than verified exact chapter titles — treat the later chapter breakdown as lower-confidence than the earlier one. Quotes are drawn from publisher/promotional material rather than independently verified against the original text page-by-page.
